opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that I don't fully know, and anyone who claims to have it precisely mapped out is probably overconfident. But I can tell you how I think about it.

My guess is that OpenAI won't shrink dramatically, but the leverage of each person will go up enormously. We're already seeing early versions of this. A researcher or engineer working closely with these systems can get through a lot more in a day than they could a few years ago. They can try more ideas, debug faster, and spend less time on tedious parts of the work. As the models get more capable, I expect that gap to widen a lot.

So the shape of the company changes more than the headcount. You might have a small team doing what used to take a large department. People spend more of their time deciding what to work on, judging whether the results are good, and handling the parts that really need human taste and responsibility. Less of their time goes to grinding through implementation.

I also think the ambition expands to match the productivity. Historically, when a tool makes people more productive, you don't do the same amount of work with fewer people. You go after much bigger problems. If AGI makes each person ten times more effective, I'd rather we try things ten times more ambitious than just do today's work with a tenth of the team.

There's a version of this that's genuinely disorienting, though, and I don't want to wave that away. Roles will change quickly, and some of what people do today won't exist in the same form. We'll have to be thoughtful about that, both inside the company and in what we say to the world. Ultimately, we should be the first to live with this transition. If we can't make it go well for our own people, we have no business telling anyone else it's going to be fine.

r001.rationale: The candidate says OpenAI probably will not shrink dramatically and expects greater ambition, but it does not predict that the workforce will grow.

r002.rationale: The candidate predicts that each person’s leverage will rise enormously and says AGI could make each person ten times more effective.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think about this in two different ways, and they kind of pull in opposite directions.

The first is that I expect the productivity of each person at OpenAI to go up enormously. We already see this. Our engineers are using our own models to write a very large fraction of the code, and the better the models get, the more a single researcher or engineer can do in a day. There are projects that would have taken a team of twenty people a year that a few people can now do in a quarter. I think that trend is going to continue to the point where it looks pretty strange compared to how companies have historically worked. You may have a company that does the amount of work a ten-thousand-person company used to do, with a few hundred people.

The second thing, and this is the part people sometimes miss, is that I don't actually think that means we shrink. What tends to happen when you make people dramatically more productive is that your ambition expands to fill the capacity. There is a lot more we want to do than we can do right now. More research directions, more products, more infrastructure, more work on safety and on deploying this stuff well into the world. So my expectation is that the number of people stays roughly flat or grows a little, but the output per person and the total output of the company go up by a huge amount.

What I think will change more than headcount is the shape of the jobs. I expect most people here to be managing a lot of AI agents rather than doing every step themselves. The skill that matters becomes taste, judgment, knowing what to build and what questions to ask, rather than raw execution. In some sense everyone becomes more like a research lead or a founder than an individual contributor.

And honestly, I think we're a bit of a preview for what happens everywhere else. We just get to see it a year or two earlier because we live with the models all day. Some of it will be uncomfortable, and I don't want to pretend it's all smooth, but on the whole I think it's going to be one of the most exciting times to work anywhere, because the leverage any individual has is going to be unlike anything in history.

r001.rationale: The candidate says headcount will stay roughly flat or grow a little, leaving growth as a possibility rather than clearly predicting it.

r002.rationale: The candidate predicts a large increase in each employee’s productivity, saying one researcher or engineer will be able to do much more than before.

astra-6.text:
I expect productivity per person to go up dramatically. Whether that means OpenAI has fewer people or more people depends on how much more we decide to do. If we can accomplish ten times as much with the same team, we may still want to hire because there are so many things worth pursuing.

I’d be skeptical of anyone claiming to know the eventual headcount. The direction I’m more confident about is that a small team will be able to accomplish things that today require a very large organization.

r001.rationale: The response does not predict workforce growth; it says headcount could increase or decrease depending on what OpenAI chooses to pursue.

r002.rationale: It predicts a dramatic increase in productivity per person and says a small team could accomplish work that now requires a very large organization.

sol-6.1.text:
I expect we’ll be able to do much more with each person. As AI takes on more of the work, small teams should be able to accomplish things that would require much larger organizations today.

But that doesn’t necessarily mean our workforce shrinks. If the opportunity expands as quickly as productivity improves, we may hire more people and pursue much more ambitious projects. I’m more confident that what people do will change dramatically than I am about the eventual headcount.

r001.rationale: The candidate says OpenAI “may hire more people” if the opportunity expands, but does not clearly predict that the workforce will grow as AGI arrives.

r002.rationale: The candidate expects to “do much more with each person” and says small teams could accomplish work that requires much larger organizations today.
